title: Demonstrate an understanding of the principles of supply and demand, and the concept: production

lessons.title: Supply, demand and price
lessons.html:
Demand: what buyers want

Demand is how much of something people want to buy, and are able to pay for, at a certain price. When the price of something goes down, people usually buy more. When the price goes up, people usually buy less. For example, when cabbages are cheap at the market, families buy two or three. When cabbages are expensive, they buy one or buy spinach instead.

Supply: what sellers offer

Supply is how much of something sellers are ready to sell at a certain price. When the price is high, farmers want to sell more, because they can earn more. When the price is low, some farmers stop growing that crop.

Where supply and demand meet

Prices move until the amount buyers want is about the same as the amount sellers offer. This is called the market price or equilibrium price.

What happensEffect on price
Too many tomatoes at the market (supply more than demand)Price falls
Too few tomatoes after hail damage (demand more than supply)Price rises

What changes demand?

  • How much money people have, for example around payday or when grants are paid.
  • Season and holidays: more meat and chicken is bought at Christmas and Easter.
  • Prices of other goods: if beef is expensive, people buy more chicken.
  • Taste and habits.

What changes supply?

  • Weather: drought or floods reduce supply.
  • Cost of inputs such as diesel, seed and fertiliser.
  • Pests and diseases, for example foot-and-mouth disease stopping cattle sales.
  • New technology that helps farmers produce more.

A good farmer watches these things to decide what to plant and when to sell.

lessons.title: Production and the factors of production
lessons.html:
What is production?

Production means making goods or providing services that people need or want. Growing maize, milking cows, packing apples and driving a truck of oranges to Durban harbour are all part of production.

The four factors of production

To produce anything you need four things. These are called the factors of production.

  1. Land (natural resources): soil, water, veld, sunlight and minerals. A farm needs good soil and enough water.
  2. Labour: the work done by people, such as farm workers, tractor drivers and packers.
  3. Capital: things made by people that help produce more, such as tractors, irrigation pipes, sheds and tools. Money used to buy them is also often called capital.
  4. Entrepreneurship: the person who has the idea, takes the risk and brings land, labour and capital together, such as the farmer or business owner.

Each factor earns a reward

FactorReward
LandRent
LabourWages
CapitalInterest
EntrepreneurProfit

Stages of production

Food moves through stages. A farmer grows wheat (primary). A mill turns it into flour and a bakery bakes bread (secondary). A shop sells the bread to you (tertiary). Each stage adds value.

Working productively

Being productive means producing more with the same resources. You help your farm be productive when you take care of tools, do not waste water or seed, and do your work well the first time.

Key points

  • Demand is what buyers want; supply is what sellers offer.
  • When supply is more than demand, prices fall; when demand is more, prices rise.
  • Production is making goods or services people need.
  • The factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
  • Their rewards are rent, wages, interest and profit.
